pieces.title: Resolution 1 — Why a separate language, and how it was wired to the page
pieces.content:
You asked four things. This takes them in order, all the way down.

Part 0 — What actually happened when you clicked something in 1994

Before the objection can be answered, the cost you are trying to avoid has to be real rather than asserted. Here is the full physical sequence when a user submitted a form.

The browser opens a TCP connection to the server. TCP requires a three-way handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — before a single byte of your data moves. That is one full round trip spent agreeing to talk.

Then the browser sends the request. A form submission is encoded as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, which is where the familiar shape comes from:

POST /cgi-bin/register.pl HTTP/1.0
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 52

name=Devansh&email=devansh%40example&city=Noida

The server passes this to a CGI program — Common Gateway Interface, from NCSA httpd in 1993. The web server spawns an entirely new operating-system process, hands it the form data, waits for it to print a complete HTML page to standard output, and sends that back. A fresh process per submission.

That program checks the email, finds no @, and writes out a whole new page saying so. The connection closes — HTTP/1.0 had no persistent connections by default — so the next request starts from the TCP handshake again.

Now the numbers. On a 28.8 kbit/s modem, round-trip latency was typically 150–400 ms and throughput about 3.5 kilobytes per second. So: one round trip for the handshake, another to send the request, a process spawn and script run on the server, and then a modest 8 KB page taking over two seconds to transfer. Call it two and a half to four seconds, during which the browser shows a blank or half-drawn page and the user can do nothing.

Your account of the multi-error case is exactly right, including the part most people miss — the re-typing. Since the server returned a new page, whatever the user had typed was gone unless the CGI author had gone to the trouble of writing every value back into the HTML as VALUE="..." attributes. Many did not. So a wrong email address could cost you the whole form.

Four errors found one at a time, at three seconds each, with re-typing in between, is a minute of a person's life to discover a missing @ — a check taking a computer roughly a microsecond, on a machine already on their desk, already holding the data.

That gap — microseconds of work, seconds of waiting, on data already local — is the entire reason this node exists.

Part 1 — Your objection, taken seriously

First, what is true. HTML 2.0 — RFC 1866, November 1995 — standardised the form controls, and they predate JavaScript; forms had been in Mosaic since 1993. So <input>, <select>, <textarea>, checkboxes, radio buttons and submit buttons were all there before any script existed.

Two corrections. <dialog> is HTML5, standardised around 2014 — not part of the 1995 picture. And lists are not interactivity; they are structure.

Now the distinction that resolves the objection: HTML gives you controls. It does not give you behaviour.

A checkbox exists; a user ticks it. Exactly two things can follow, both decided by the browser: it redraws the box with a tick, and on submission that value is included in what goes to the server. There is no third. You cannot express "when this is ticked, reveal those fields," or "if this box lacks an @, say so." Each needs a condition — if this, then that — and HTML has no grammar for conditions.

HTML is declarative: it declares what things are. <input type="text"> says "a text box exists here." There is no place in that sentence to attach "and when something happens, do this."

The sharpest way to see it: in 1995 the only thing a page could do in response to user input was submit a form. The entire interactive vocabulary of the web was fill in fields, press submit, wait, receive a new page. Every interaction, however trivial, was a page navigation.

Part 2 — Why not just add conditions to HTML? They did, twice, and neither worked

Attempt one: more attributes — which actually happened

About twenty years later, HTML5 added exactly what you are describing:

<input type="email" required>
<input type="text" pattern="[0-9]{6}" title="Six digits">
<input type="number" min="1" max="10">

Get it wrong and the browser blocks submission and shows a message, with no JavaScript. Your instinct was sound enough that the standards process eventually agreed with it.

And yet almost every real form still validates in JavaScript. Watch what happens as requirements leave the pre-built list: required only if another box is ticked; two fields that must match; a username checked against the server as you type; the error shown beside the field in your own styling and language; a date at least eighteen years ago; three values whose total must not exceed a fourth.

None are expressible as attributes. And the fix shows why the approach cannot work. You would need required-if, then must-match, then min-age, then sum-max — a new attribute for every requirement anyone has ever had. Each must be proposed to a standards body, agreed by every vendor, implemented separately, and then waited out until enough users have a browser that supports it. In the 1990s that wait was measured in years, because browsers shipped on CDs.

So the vocabulary grows without bound and is always behind what people need. The alternative is one thing that can express any behaviour — variables, conditions, the ability to receive new instructions without shipping a new browser. That is what a programming language is.

Notice the shift in power. With attributes, the browser vendor decides what is possible and you wait. With a language, you decide, and ship it today, in the same file.

Attempt two: Java applets — the alternative that shipped and lost

In 1995 the obvious answer to "the web needs programs" was not a new language. It was Java, announced by Sun in May 1995 with enormous force. Netscape Navigator 2.0 shipped with a Java virtual machine built in. Java applets — real compiled programs running inside the page — were the future everyone expected.

They failed for reasons that map precisely onto your question.

They started slowly. The JVM had to initialise before anything ran; users watched a grey rectangle for several seconds, on a connection already costing seconds per page.

They needed a compile step. You wrote .java, compiled to .class bytecode, uploaded it. You could not open the page source and adjust something. The audience — writers, designers, academics — was locked out.

And decisively: they could not touch the page. An applet was a rectangle. The browser handed it a box of pixels and it drew inside. It could not read your form's text box, could not change the heading, could not hide a paragraph. It was a separate program parked on the page, not part of it.

That is exactly what you were reaching for when you asked how a script could control parts of the screen. Applets could not, and that is why they lost. What was needed was something that started instantly, needed no compilation, was editable by non-programmers, and could reach into the page the browser had already built. Eich's brief was explicitly a companion to Java: Java for serious components, a small scripting language for the page. The small one turned out to be the one people needed.

There was a third attempt. Microsoft shipped VBScript alongside its JavaScript clone (JScript) in Internet Explorer 3.0, August 1996. It only ever worked in Internet Explorer, so writing it meant abandoning half your audience. It died on the web and survived only inside corporate intranets that mandated IE.

Part 3 — How the script was joined to the page

Three mechanisms, all in Netscape Navigator 2.0 — beta as LiveScript in September 1995, renamed JavaScript on 4 December 1995, released March 1996.

Mechanism 1: the code lived inside the page

You pictured two files. In 1995 it was usually one:

<HTML>
<HEAD>
<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript">
<!--
function checkEmail() {
  var v = document.reg.email.value;
  if (v.indexOf("@") == -1) {
    alert("Please enter a valid email address.");
    return false;
  }
  return true;
}
// -->
</SCRIPT>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<FORM NAME="reg" ACTION="/cgi-bin/register.pl" METHOD="POST"
      onSubmit="return checkEmail()">
  <INPUT TYPE="text" NAME="email">
  <INPUT TYPE="submit" VALUE="Send">
</FORM>
</BODY>
</HTML>

Period-accurate, down to the uppercase tags. That is your form-validation example, working, in 1996.

Now the <!-- and // -->. That is an HTML comment wrapping the code. Browsers that had never heard of <script> — in 1996, most of them — follow a rule that says ignore tags you do not recognise, but render their contents. Without the comment, those users saw the source code printed on the page as text. The comment made old browsers skip it, while browsers that understood <script> knew to ignore the markers. The // is needed because --> is not valid JavaScript — the comment has to be hidden from the script engine as well as shown to the parser. Two languages negotiating in three characters.

Note what that trick is: a workaround so a new capability does not break the experience for software that predates it. Hold that thought for Part 5.

Mechanism 2: attributes whose value is code

Here is the actual bridge:

<FORM NAME="reg" onSubmit="return checkEmail()">

onSubmit sits in the markup like NAME or TYPE. But its value is neither text nor a number — it is JavaScript source. The browser stores that string and, when the form is submitted, executes it.

Mechanically, the browser takes the attribute's string and effectively wraps it in a function:

function (event) { return checkEmail(); }

That is not a metaphor — it is why return false works there but would be a syntax error at the top level of a script. The attribute's contents are a function body.

Netscape 2.0 shipped a small family: onClick, onSubmit, onChange, onFocus, onBlur, onMouseOver, onLoad. Markup declares structure; a handful of attributes hand specific moments to the script.

Two consequences that resurface later in the chain. The return value is meaningful — onSubmit inspects it, and false cancels the submission. That is what stops the round trip from Part 0; the browser never opens a socket. And this inside the handler is the element: in onClick="this.value='clicked'", this is the button. That is the origin of the DOM half of Node 5's this rules — the browser calls your handler with the element bound as the receiver.

Mechanism 3: the page as objects the script can reach

The deepest part, and the direct answer: the script does not control the screen. It cannot draw. It has no access to pixels.

What happens is that the browser, while parsing the HTML, builds objects in memory representing what it found. A <form> becomes a form object; an <input> becomes an object with a value property. The script reads and writes those objects, and the browser redraws from them.

document.reg.email.value

means: on document, find the form named reg; on it, the input named email; read its value. Three property lookups. No pixels anywhere.

In 1995 that object model was crude and fixed — retroactively called DOM Level 0. You got a handful of collections: document.forms, document.images, document.links, document.anchors, document.title, window.location.

There was no getElementById — that came with the W3C's DOM Level 1 in October 1998. No creating elements, no changing arbitrary text, no restructuring. You could read and write form values, swap document.images[0].src (how every 1990s rollover worked), and write text into the page while it was still loading.

The asymmetry is worth stating plainly, because it explains the shape of the whole first decade: the script could read and modify things that already existed, but could not create structure. Anything you wanted to change had to be in the HTML already, sitting hidden. That is why 1990s pages are full of hidden elements toggled into view, and why "dynamic HTML" felt like a trick rather than a capability until DOM Level 1 arrived.

Part 4 — Why a script blocked the page from rendering

The browser's pipeline runs roughly:

bytes → tokenizer → parser → object tree (DOM) → layout → paint

The tokenizer chews the HTML into tokens; the parser assembles them into the object tree; layout computes where everything sits; paint draws it. This is a stream — the browser starts drawing before the file has finished arriving, which is why 1990s pages appeared progressively, top-down.

Now the parser reaches <script>. It must decide: keep parsing while the script runs, or stop? It has no choice but to stop, because of this:

<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript">
document.write("<P>Hello, it is " + new Date() + "</P>");
</SCRIPT>

document.write does not modify the finished page. It injects raw text into the tokenizer's input stream at the exact position the parser has reached. The parser then tokenizes what the script just wrote as though it had been in the file all along.

So the parser cannot advance past a <script> before running it — the script may be about to hand it more source. Worse, the script can write an unbalanced fragment such as document.write("<TABLE><TR><TD>"), leaving the parser mid-element with the rest of the file completing the structure. Parsing ahead speculatively is therefore not merely wasteful but incorrect.

That is the architectural fact you were reaching for. It is not that anyone feared scripts freezing pages; it is that document.write's design made blocking mandatory. And because parsing blocks, the object tree stops growing, so layout stops, so paint stops. A slow script is a page that has stopped appearing.

This is not history. Put a slow <script src="…"> in the <head> today and you get a white screen until it loads — still the most common cause of slow-feeling sites. The escapes came later, and both are promises not to use document.write: defer (HTML 4.0, December 1997) keeps parsing and runs the script after the document is parsed, in order; async (HTML5) keeps parsing and runs it whenever it arrives. Both exist solely because the default had to be blocking.

And now the connection forward. The chain runs: document.write exists → the parser must block on scripts → a slow script freezes the page → "never block the page" becomes a hard constraint on the language. The single thread, the callbacks, the event loop you meet at Node 9 — the entire second half of the language — descends from a rule established here in 1995, by a function almost nobody uses any more.

Part 5 — Two places where I was loose, and you caught one

In the landscape I listed four constraints as one family. Three genuinely belong together — start instantly, do not touch the machine, do not freeze the page — because all three follow from this code arrived from a stranger and runs on your computer.

"Never break old pages" is not in that family. It has nothing to do with trust. It comes from a different property of the web: publish once, abandon forever.

Installed software has an update path: the vendor ships version 2, you update. The web has none. A page published in 1997 is still served, byte for byte, by a machine nobody has logged into in fifteen years, written by someone unreachable. If a browser changes how it interprets something, that page breaks permanently, with no possible remedy — and a browser that breaks pages loses users to one that does not. The pressure is commercial as much as technical.

That is why the language can only add, never change, and why you have three ways to declare a variable — which is what your Q4 and Q5 push on, and which deserves its own piece.

The second correction — your sandbox guess

Your reasoning is sound but the history runs the other way. Tabs did not exist in 1995. Tabbed browsing arrived with Opera and the Mozilla suite around 2000–2003. And process isolation — each tab as a separate operating-system process, so one crashing or being compromised cannot reach another — came with Google Chrome in 2008, thirteen years later. Site isolation is later still, hardened after the Spectre disclosures in 2018.

So the 1995 "sandbox" was far weaker than you pictured. It was not enforced by the operating system. It was enforced by absence: the language simply had no filesystem API, no process API, no network API beyond fetching a URL. You could not open a file because there was no function that opened files. Security by not providing the capability.

The one genuine security boundary from that era is the same-origin policy, introduced in Netscape 2.0 in 1995, and it is the real ancestor of what you were describing: a script from bank.com cannot read the contents of a page from mail.com, even if both are open. Without it, any page you visited could read your webmail. That policy is why CORS exists.

So your instinct that isolation matters was right; the mechanism you attributed it to arrived thirteen years later.

Part 6 — What using it was actually like

The code was plain text in the page, delivered as-is. Anyone could choose View → Source and read the complete working source of every script on any site. No compilation, no minification, no build step. If you liked what a page did, you read exactly how, and pasted it into your file.

That is how essentially everyone learned JavaScript for its first decade — not from books, from view-source. Enormous numbers of pages ran near-identical validation snippets propagated by copy-paste, mutating slightly at each hop. The same three or four scripts, subtly corrupted, ran on thousands of sites.

It also compounds the ten days from Node 0: whatever shipped was immediately and permanently visible to everyone, and being copied within days. There was no quiet window in which to fix it.

And then it got standardised anyway. Microsoft reverse-engineered the language for Internet Explorer 3.0 in August 1996, calling it JScript to avoid Sun's trademark. Two independent implementations of an undocumented language immediately began to diverge, and pages started working in one browser and not the other. Netscape submitted the language to Ecma International in November 1996, and ECMA-262 edition 1 was published in June 1997.

Which means the ten-day design was frozen into an international standard within eighteen months, at a moment when nobody could yet see which parts were mistakes. That is the mechanism by which a rushed prototype became permanent.

What this resolves

Your follow-upWhat answers it
Q1 — why not extend HTML?Parts 1–2: HTML gives controls, not behaviour. They did add validation attributes twenty years later and it still is not enough. Applets were the serious alternative and lost.
Q1 — how were script and page connected?Part 3: <script> inside the page, event attributes whose value is a function body, and an object tree the script reads and writes
Q1 — what did it actually look like?Parts 3 and 6: period code, the comment-wrapping trick, view-source culture
Q1 — why was the round trip so bad?Part 0: TCP handshake, CGI process spawn, HTTP/1.0 without keep-alive, ~3 s per attempt, and re-typing the form each time
Q7 — how could a script affect rendering?Part 4: document.write injects into the tokenizer stream, so blocking is mandatory rather than cautious
Q7 — sandboxing and tab isolationPart 5: right instinct, wrong mechanism — tabs are ~2001, process isolation is Chrome 2008. The 1995 boundary was the same-origin policy and the absence of dangerous APIs.
Q7 — how does "never break old pages" relate to untrusted code?Part 5: it does not. My framing conflated two different pressures.

Seven distinct doubts, one explanation.

pieces.title: Resolution 2 — Q1: the two files, the actual format, and what an author actually did
pieces.content:
This is Q1's follow-up on its own. Resolution 1 was written across Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q7 together, and it answered two of the things you asked here — why HTML could not simply be extended, and how a script inside the page was joined to it. Re-reading your follow-up against it, four of your asks were not answered, and one of them I contradicted rather than answered. Those are what this piece is for.

The asks I find in your follow-up, in the order you raised them:

  1. HTML already gives interactivity — buttons, lists, dialog boxes, tick boxes — so why a separate language? (Resolution 1, Parts 1 and 2. Not repeated here; one thing added at the end.)
  2. Your account of the 1994 form round trip — is it right? (Resolution 1, Part 0. It is right, including the part most people miss.)
  3. "Supposedly there were two files" — an HTML file and a separate script file. How were those two joined? Resolution 1 told you it was usually one file and moved on. That dodged the question. Section 1 below.
  4. "I really want to know the actual format" — what the thing literally looked like on disk, in the tag, and on the wire. Section 2.
  5. How was the script "able to control certain parts of the screen" — specifically certain parts. What was reachable, what was not, and how a script named the part it wanted. Section 3.
  6. "How the browser actually carried out all of the stuff" — the engine itself. What ran your source, and how a string in an attribute became a running function. Section 4.
  7. "How people actually used it" — the workflow. What a person in 1996 actually did to write and debug this. Section 5.

Section 1 — The two files: <SCRIPT SRC>, and the year you could not have it

Resolution 1 said "you pictured two files; in 1995 it was usually one" and went on to the inline case. That is true but it is not an answer, because you asked how two files get joined, and two files is how every page you have ever written works. Here is the actual mechanism and its actual history.

The joining mechanism is one attribute:

<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript" SRC="/js/validate.js"></SCRIPT>

Three things about that line are worth pulling apart, because each is a decision that is still live today.

First: the closing tag is mandatory and the element must be empty. <SCRIPT SRC="..." /> does not work and never has. If you write it, the parser does not close the element — it keeps consuming the rest of your document as script source until it finds a literal </script>, and everything after your self-closed tag silently vanishes from the page. This is not a browser bug. HTML is not XML; only a fixed list of elements (<br>, <img>, <input> and a handful more) are void, and <script> is not one of them. The trailing slash is ignored as a stray attribute. This is one of the oldest still-active foot-guns in web development.

Second: if SRC is present, any content between the tags is ignored. You cannot use the inline body as a fallback for a failed download. One script element is either an external script or an inline script, never both.

Third — and this is the part that answers your history question: you could not do this in the first release. Netscape Navigator 2.0, which shipped in March 1996 as the first browser with JavaScript in it, did not support SRC on <SCRIPT>. There was no such thing as a .js file on the web. Every line of JavaScript on Earth lived inside the HTML document that used it.

SRC arrived with Netscape Navigator 3.0, August 1996, alongside LANGUAGE="JavaScript1.1". So the two-file world you are imagining is not the starting point of the story — it is a feature added roughly nine months in, and it took a further year or two before authors could rely on it, because a page using SRC simply had no script at all in Navigator 2.0.

That gap matters for the way you framed the question. You assumed two files and asked how they were connected. The real sequence is the reverse: one file was the design, and separating them was the improvement — which raises the more interesting question of why anyone bothered to add SRC at all, given that inline scripts already worked perfectly.

Three reasons, and they are the same three reasons you still put JavaScript in a separate file today.

Caching. This is the dominant one, and on a 28.8 kbit/s modem it was not a nicety. An HTML page is different on every URL — the product page and the checkout page are different documents. The validation code is identical on both. Inline, the user downloads it again on every page, at roughly 3.5 kilobytes per second. External, the browser sends the second request with a conditional header:

GET /js/validate.js HTTP/1.0
If-Modified-Since: Tue, 06 Aug 1996 12:00:00 GMT

and the server answers 304 Not Modified with an empty body. A 12 KB library downloaded once instead of once per page is, at 1996 speeds, several seconds saved on every subsequent navigation. Caching is why SRC exists.

Sharing across pages without copying. Before SRC, "reuse" meant pasting the same function into forty HTML files, and fixing a bug meant editing forty files. There were no build tools, no includes, no templating in the browser. Server-side includes (SSI) existed in NCSA httpd and could stitch a common block into each page, but that solved the authoring problem while making the caching problem worse — the code still travelled down the wire with every page.

The document stays readable. A secondary benefit at the time, and the seed of an idea — structure in one place, behaviour in another — that took until the mid-2000s to become an explicit principle ("unobtrusive JavaScript"), and until frameworks in the 2010s to be partially reversed again.

One more mechanism belongs here, because it is a third way a script was joined to a page and it is older than SRC: the javascript: URL scheme, present from Navigator 2.0.

<A HREF="javascript:document.reg.submit()">Send the form</A>

Here the code is not in a <SCRIPT> element and not in an event attribute — it is in the address of a link. The browser's URL resolver recognises the javascript: scheme, and instead of fetching anything it evaluates the rest of the string and, if the result is a string, replaces the document with it. That is a whole pseudo-protocol invented so that a link could run code. It still works in the address bar's absence today only in a degraded form — every major browser now strips javascript: when pasted into the URL bar, precisely because it was the easiest way to talk a person into running an attacker's code on their own banking session. A capability added in 1995 for convenience became an attack vector and was walked back thirty years later; you will meet that pattern repeatedly in this landscape.

Section 2 — The actual format: on disk, inside the tag, and on the wire

You said you want to know "the actual format." Take that literally in three layers.

On disk, there is no format. A JavaScript file is a plain text file. No header, no magic bytes, no manifest, no declared version, no entry point, no imports. The .js extension is a convention that the web server uses to guess a MIME type; nothing in the language requires it and nothing checks it. Contrast this with a Java applet, which was .class bytecode with a four-byte magic number (CA FE BA BE), a constant pool, and a declared class structure — a file that announces what it is. A .js file announces nothing. It is source, and the whole of its meaning is produced at the moment a browser reads it.

Inside the tag, the format is a set of attributes that have changed twice. Period-accurate 1996:

<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript">

LANGUAGE was the original attribute, and its job was to say which language this was — because in 1996 the answer was genuinely in doubt. Internet Explorer 3.0, August 1996, shipped two script engines, and pages in the wild really did contain:

<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="VBScript">
Sub btn_OnClick
  MsgBox "Hello"
End Sub
</SCRIPT>

Then LANGUAGE acquired a second job that is worth understanding, because it is a beautiful and ugly piece of engineering. Netscape 3.0 introduced version suffixes:

<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript">
  var canDoImages = false;
</SCRIPT>
<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript1.1">
  var canDoImages = true;
</SCRIPT>

The rule a browser follows is: if I do not recognise the value of LANGUAGE, I skip this element entirely. Navigator 2.0 has never heard of JavaScript1.1, so it skips the second block and canDoImages stays false. Navigator 3.0 understands it, runs it, and the variable becomes true. That is feature detection performed by the HTML parser, with no if statement anywhere, and it is how 1996–1998 pages shipped image rollovers to browsers that supported the Image object without breaking browsers that did not. JavaScript1.2 gated Navigator 4.0 features the same way.

Note what this is: the same shape as the <!-- comment trick from Resolution 1 — new capability, wrapped so that software which predates it degrades quietly instead of breaking. Two different mechanisms, one pressure.

HTML 4.0 (December 1997) deprecated LANGUAGE and replaced it with TYPE, carrying a MIME type rather than a name:

<script type="text/javascript">

which was the correct-looking incantation everyone typed for the next fifteen years. HTML5 then made it unnecessary — <script> with no attributes means JavaScript — and type came back with an entirely different job, which is to say this is not a classic script: type="module" (ES2015 modules, shipped in browsers 2017), type="application/json" and type="text/template" for inert data the parser must not execute. So the attribute went from "which language" to "which MIME type" to "which execution mode."

On the wire, the format is an HTTP response, and the header matters more than the file. When the browser fetches /js/validate.js it receives:

HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: Tue, 06 Aug 1996 12:00:00 GMT
Server: NCSA/1.5.2
Content-Type: application/x-javascript
Content-Length: 1043

function checkEmail() { ... }

That Content-Type is the browser's only reliable statement of what it just received, and it is set by the server, from its extension-to-MIME table — in NCSA and early Apache, a mime.types file. A server that had not been told about .js served it as text/plain or application/octet-stream, and the browser would decline to execute it or offer it as a download. "It works locally but not on the server" was already a category of bug in 1996, and the cause was a line missing from a config file.

The MIME type itself has an untidy history worth knowing because you will still see all of it in real codebases. Netscape used application/x-javascript; the x- prefix meant "experimental, not registered with IANA." text/javascript became the de facto standard by weight of use. RFC 4329, April 2006, tried to clean this up: it registered application/javascript as correct and declared text/javascript obsolete. The web ignored it — every page on Earth already said text/javascript — and the WHATWG eventually surrendered and re-blessed text/javascript as the standard type. A rare, clean case of the specification losing to reality and being rewritten to match.

One consequence of "there is no format" that bites to this day: a .js file has no declared character encoding. There is no equivalent of the <meta charset> you put in HTML. An external script inherits the encoding of the document that included it, unless the response carries an explicit charset parameter. Include a UTF-8 script from a Latin-1 page and every non-ASCII string literal in it is silently corrupted. This is why the charset attribute existed on <script>, and why the modern advice is to serve everything as UTF-8 and never think about it again.

Section 3 — "Certain parts of the screen": what a script could reach, and what it could not

Your phrasing was precise and I want to hold you to it: how could the script control certain parts of the screen. Resolution 1 answered the "not the screen" half — the script touches objects, the browser draws. It did not answer the certain parts half, which is the question of addressing. How does a script say this element and not that one?

In 1996 the answer is: by name, and only for the few kinds of thing the browser bothered to name.

When the parser encountered <FORM NAME="reg">, it did two things: it created a form object, and it registered that object as a property of document under the string in NAME. Same for <INPUT NAME="email"> inside it — registered as a property of the form object. So this chain:

document.reg.email.value

is three ordinary property lookups on three ordinary objects, and the "addressing" is nothing more than the author and the browser having agreed on a string. There is no query, no selector engine, no search of the tree. Names go in, names come out.

The complete list of what DOM Level 0 exposed is short enough to write out, and its shortness is the point:

document.forms[]      document.reg
document.images[]     document.links[]
document.anchors[]    document.applets[]
document.embeds[]     document.title
document.location     document.cookie
document.lastModified document.referrer
window.location       window.status
window.history        window.navigator

Now look at what is not there. There is no document.paragraphs. No document.headings, no document.tables, no document.divs. A <P> in the page was not addressable at all — not by name, not by index, not by any route. The text you were reading on screen was, from the script's point of view, unreachable.

That is why the honest answer to "how did the script control certain parts of the screen" in 1996 is: it mostly could not. It could control exactly four categories of thing —

  • Form control values — read them, write them, and cancel the submission. Which is why the canonical first use of JavaScript was form validation: not because validation is the most interesting problem, but because form fields were nearly the only objects that existed.
  • Image sources — document.images[0].src = "on.gif". Swap the URL and the browser refetches and repaints that rectangle. Every mouse-over highlight on the 1990s web is this one line, usually with new Image() preloading added in Navigator 3.0 so the swap did not flicker while the replacement downloaded.
  • The window and its address — window.location = "..." to navigate, window.open(...) for the pop-up, window.status to write into the status bar at the bottom of the browser chrome. Note that this is not the page at all; it is the browser's own furniture.
  • The document as it was being built — document.write, which as Resolution 1 covered injects into the tokenizer stream. This was the only way to affect arbitrary page content, and it worked only during parsing. Call it after the page finished loading and it implicitly opens a fresh document and wipes everything.

So the shape of the first three years of the language is set by an addressing limitation, not by a language limitation. Everything you know as DOM manipulation is absent.

The escape came in 1997–1998, and it came as a schism rather than a feature, which is itself the answer to part of your last question about how people actually worked:

Netscape Navigator 4.0 (June 1997) invented a new element, <LAYER>, a positionable box, and exposed document.layers["name"]. Only layers were addressable; ordinary elements still were not.

Internet Explorer 4.0 (September 1997) did something far more radical: it exposed every element, via document.all["name"], and gave every one of them a property that let you replace its contents with a string of HTML:

document.all.greeting.innerHTML = "<B>Hello, "  + name + "</B>";

innerHTML is a Microsoft invention from 1997. It was not in any standard. It was so obviously the thing everyone wanted that it was reverse-engineered by every other browser, and it was finally standardised — fourteen years after it shipped — in the DOM Parsing specification around 2011. You use it constantly; it entered the platform as a proprietary extension in a browser war.

The W3C's answer to both was DOM Level 1, October 1998: getElementById, createElement, appendChild, a real tree with real node types, and every element addressable by standard means. That is the moment the asymmetry in Resolution 1 — "you can modify what exists but not create structure" — finally ends, and it is three years after the language shipped.

Section 4 — What the browser actually did: the engine, and how a string became a function

You asked how the browser "actually carried out all of the stuff." Two mechanisms answer that: what executed your source, and what happened to the code sitting inside an onSubmit attribute.

The engine. The first implementation was written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in May 1995, in about ten days, under the internal codename Mocha. It was renamed LiveScript for the Navigator 2.0 betas in September 1995, and JavaScript on 4 December 1995, in a joint Netscape/Sun press release — a marketing decision to borrow the momentum of Java, which is the origin of thirty years of people assuming the two languages are related. They are not; the shared syntax of curly braces and for loops comes from C, and the semantics — first-class functions, prototypes, dynamic types — come from Scheme and Self.

Mocha was replaced in 1996 by a rewrite, also by Eich, in C, which is SpiderMonkey — still the engine in Firefox today, thirty years on. Microsoft shipped an independent clone called JScript in Internet Explorer 3.0, August 1996, reverse-engineered rather than licensed, which is what triggered the standardisation effort: Netscape took the language to Ecma International, and ECMA-262 1st edition was ratified in June 1997. The name "ECMAScript" exists because "JavaScript" was a Sun trademark that neither the standards body nor Microsoft could use.

What the engine did with your source, in outline, and the outline is the important part:

source text
   → lexer      (characters → tokens)
   → parser     (tokens → syntax tree)
   → bytecode generator
   → interpreter loop  (fetch opcode, execute, repeat)

Every one of those stages happened at page load, on the user's machine, every time the page was opened, with the result thrown away when the page closed. Nothing was cached in compiled form.

And critically: there was no compilation to machine code anywhere in this picture until 2008. For the first thirteen years of the language's life, every browser executed JavaScript by interpreting bytecode in a loop. This is why JavaScript's reputation for the whole of that period was "toy language, unusably slow for anything real," and why serious computation in the browser meant an applet or a Flash movie. Google's V8 (September 2008, with Chrome) and Mozilla's TraceMonkey the same year introduced just-in-time compilation to native code, and the language got roughly an order of magnitude faster in about eighteen months. Everything you take for granted — that you can run a build tool, a spreadsheet, a video editor in JavaScript — is downstream of a change made thirteen years after the language was designed. When you reach the performance material later in the landscape, keep that date: the language was designed for an interpreter and is now run on a JIT, and several things that look like arbitrary rules are really the JIT's requirements leaking upward.

How the attribute string became a function. This is the mechanism you were circling when you asked how the script "controls" a part of the page. Take:

<FORM NAME="reg" onSubmit="return checkEmail()">

When the parser builds the form object, it sees an attribute whose name begins with on and which matches its list of known event names. It does not store text. It hands the string to the script engine to be compiled as a function body — the equivalent of:

form.onsubmit = new Function("event", "return checkEmail()");

and stores the resulting function object on the element as a property. Three consequences follow directly, and all three still hold in 2026:

A syntax error in the attribute is discovered at parse time, not at click time, because compilation happens when the element is created.

return is legal there — and is a syntax error at the top level of a <script> block — because the attribute's contents genuinely are a function body. Resolution 1 mentioned this; the reason is that it is literally compiled as one.

The function is called with the element as its receiver. When the form is submitted, the browser looks up form.onsubmit and invokes it as a method of the element, which is what makes this inside an inline handler refer to the element. This is the substrate of the DOM half of the this rules you meet in Node 5 — not a special case in the language, just an ordinary method call that the browser happens to make on your behalf.

What "dispatch" meant in 1996, and what it did not. There was one handler slot per element per event. Assigning form.onsubmit a second time silently discarded the first — two independent scripts on one page could not both listen to the same button. There was no propagation model at all: the event went to the element, and that was the whole story. Netscape 4 then added capturing (events travel down from the window) and IE4 added bubbling (events travel up from the target), incompatibly and in opposite directions, so 1997–2000 code frequently implemented both. DOM Level 2 Events (November 2000) reconciled them into the model you know — capture down, target, bubble up — and introduced addEventListener, whose entire reason for existing is that it permits many listeners on one element instead of one. Every event-delegation pattern you have ever written depends on bubbling, which is a 1997 Microsoft idea standardised in 2000.

Section 5 — How a person actually worked in 1996

You asked how people actually used the scripts. This is not a footnote; the working conditions explain the shape of the code that survives from that era.

There was no tooling. None. No editor with knowledge of the language, no autocomplete, no type checking, no linter, no package manager, no build step, no bundler, no minifier, no transpiler, no source maps, no version manager, no framework. You wrote in Notepad, BBEdit or vi, saved, and hit reload.

There was no debugger and, in Navigator 2.0, no console output at all. The universal debugging technique was:

alert("got here, v = " + v);

a modal dialog that halts everything until you click OK. Debugging a loop meant clicking OK a hundred times, or restarting the browser. Netscape did expose a JavaScript console — you reached it by typing javascript: into the location bar, which opened a two-pane window showing errors and offering an evaluation box — and Navigator 4 shipped a proper script debugger, but the alert habit was so entrenched that it outlived its necessity by a decade. console.log is not part of the language even now; it arrived as a Firebug extension feature in 2006 and was standardised as a browser API long afterwards.

Errors were silent or worse. A script error typically produced a dialog box in the user's face — a real one, on a real visitor's screen, saying something like "reg" is not defined. Pages in the wild routinely shipped broken and the visitor absorbed the failure.

Learning happened by View Source, and that is not a nostalgic detail — it is the reason the language spread. Because the code was plain text inside the document, every page on the web was its own tutorial. You saw a rollover effect, chose View Source, read the whole implementation, copied it, changed the filenames. There was no other distribution mechanism: no npm, no GitHub, no Stack Overflow. There were script archives — The JavaScript Source (1996) and later Dynamic Drive (1998) — which were literally web pages with blocks of code and a "copy this into your HTML" instruction. That is what a dependency was.

Consider what this implies about who wrote JavaScript. Not, mostly, programmers. Designers, writers, students, hobbyists — people who had learned HTML by copying it, and who now copied scripts the same way. Eich's brief was explicitly to make a language for that audience: "something that looks like Java but is for people who are not programmers." The design decisions people criticise hardest — that var was optional, that undeclared assignment created a global, that types coerced silently rather than erroring, that a missing semicolon was inserted for you, that almost nothing threw — are all the same decision, made deliberately: never stop, never fail loudly, do something plausible, because the person writing this cannot debug and the person reading it did not ask for a dialog box. Those choices are the source of most of the confusion this landscape spends Nodes 3 through 6 unwinding, and they were correct for 1996 and wrong for 2026 — and, per Resolution 1's Part 5, they can never be removed, only added around. That is why let exists beside var, and why "use strict" and modules had to invent a way to opt into a stricter language rather than fixing the old one.

And there was the browser war, which is what "how people worked" really meant from 1997. With Navigator 4 and IE4 exposing incompatible object models, a working page needed both paths and a way to choose between them. The technique was browser sniffing: read the browser's self-description and branch.

var isNS4 = (document.layers) ? true : false;
var isIE4 = (document.all)    ? true : false;

function show(name) {
  if (isNS4)      document.layers[name].visibility = "show";
  else if (isIE4) document.all[name].style.visibility = "visible";
}

Every non-trivial page carried a block like that. It is why navigator.userAgent is the tangle it is today — browsers added each other's names to their user-agent strings to be let through sniffing code written for a competitor, which is why Chrome's user agent in 2026 still contains the words Mozilla, AppleWebKit, KHTML, like Gecko and Safari. That string is a fossil record of thirty years of pages guessing wrong. The lesson the industry eventually drew — test for the capability, not the browser — is why the modern idiom is if ('IntersectionObserver' in window) and never if (isChrome).

Section 6 — Where Resolution 1 was thin, on your own terms

Two things to put right, one of them mine.

Your "why not extend HTML" instinct deserves one more sentence than Resolution 1 gave it. That piece answered with the vocabulary argument — attributes cannot express arbitrary conditions, so the vocabulary grows without bound. True, but incomplete, and the missing half is the one you can feel in your own work. Even where an attribute does exist, it hands the decision to the browser vendor and hands you a wait. <input type="email" required> shipped in browsers around 2010–2012 and could not be relied on until roughly 2015 — twenty years after the need was obvious. A language lets you ship the behaviour with the page, today, to every browser at once. The argument is not only about expressiveness; it is about who controls the release schedule. That is the deeper reason a language won, and it generalises: it is the same reason every platform that started declarative eventually grew a scripting layer.

And the correction I owe you: Resolution 1 answered "how were the two files connected" by telling you there was only one file. That was a true statement used to avoid a question. Your mental model was not wrong, it was just early — the two-file arrangement you assumed became the norm from Navigator 3.0 in August 1996 and is universal now, and the mechanism joining them is the SRC attribute in Section 1. When your question contains an assumption that does not hold for the period, the right move is to date the assumption, not to drop the question.

What this resolves

HTML already has buttons and tick boxes — why a language?Resolution 1, Parts 1–2 (controls vs. behaviour; attributes vs. conditions), extended in Section 6 with the release-schedule argument
Is my account of the 1994 form round trip right?Resolution 1, Part 0 — yes, including the re-typing, which is the part usually forgotten
"Supposedly there were two files" — how were they joined?Section 1: <SCRIPT SRC>, absent from Navigator 2.0, added in Navigator 3.0 (Aug 1996) for caching, sharing and separation. Plus javascript: URLs as a third joining mechanism.
What was the actual format?Section 2: plain text with no format at all on disk; LANGUAGE → TYPE → nothing → execution mode in the tag; Content-Type on the wire, and the x-javascript / text/javascript / RFC 4329 mess
How did it control certain parts of the screen?Section 3: by NAME, and only for forms, images, links and anchors. Paragraphs were unreachable. document.layers / document.all / innerHTML in 1997, getElementById in DOM Level 1, October 1998.
How did the browser actually carry it out?Section 4: Mocha → SpiderMonkey; lex, parse, bytecode, interpreter loop, no JIT until V8 in 2008; and an onSubmit attribute compiled into a function body with the element as this
How did people actually use it?Section 5: no tooling, alert as the debugger, View Source as the package manager, script archives as dependencies, browser sniffing as the compatibility layer — and why that audience produced a language that refuses to fail loudly
Correction owedSection 6: Resolution 1 dismissed the two-file question instead of dating the assumption and answering it

Seven asks in one follow-up. Two answered previously, five answered here.

pieces.title: Resolution 3 — Q4: backwards compatibility, and everything in the language that exists because of it
pieces.content:
Your follow-up has three asks and one buried assumption that has to be dislodged first, because the assumption is the reason the constraint is as absolute as it is.

  1. Elaborate the constraint properly — what "backwards compatibility" actually means here, and who enforces it. Sections 1–2.
  2. What choices could have been made but could not be — the foreclosed design space. Section 7, with the machinery in Section 3.
  3. What is in the language today because of this — "properly, each and everything." Sections 4, 5 and 6 are the catalogue. It is long on purpose.

The assumption is in your phrasing: "only new additions could be done that could later be adopted by the community but still the previous versions also worked as well." You are describing versioning — old version keeps working, new version is available, code picks one. That is how Python, Rust, C++ and Java all work. JavaScript does not have it, has never had it, and tried twice and failed. That absence is the whole story, so it goes first.

Section 1 — The root fact: JavaScript has no versions

Every other language you will use solves this problem with a version declaration. The mechanism differs but the idea is identical: a file says which dialect it is written in, and the compiler obeys.

// Rust — in Cargo.toml
edition = "2021"

// C++ — on the command line
g++ -std=c++20 main.cpp

// Python — the file itself is 2 or 3, and they are different programs
python3 script.py

// Perl — since 1993
use strict;
use v5.36;

Rust is the sharpest comparison, because Rust deliberately solved exactly the problem JavaScript has. Rust editions — 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024 — are allowed to make breaking changes: keywords added, syntax changed, defaults reversed. async and await became reserved words in the 2018 edition, which would have broken every crate that used them as identifiers — except that a crate declares its edition, and the compiler applies the old rules to old crates and the new rules to new ones, in the same build, linked together. Rust can therefore keep fixing its own mistakes forever.

Now ask where JavaScript would put that declaration. There is nowhere. A script is a fragment of text delivered inside an HTML page from an arbitrary server. There is no project file, no manifest, no compiler invocation, no build. The browser receives bytes and must decide how to interpret them with no accompanying statement of intent.

It was tried twice.

The first attempt is the one you saw in Resolution 2: LANGUAGE="JavaScript1.1", "JavaScript1.2", "JavaScript1.3". That was a genuine version selector — Navigator 4 really did change semantics inside a JavaScript1.2 block, most notoriously making == behave differently for some comparisons. It was a disaster in exactly the way you would predict: the same source behaved differently depending on a string in an attribute, authors got the string wrong, and other browsers implemented the version numbers inconsistently or not at all. HTML 4.0 deprecated LANGUAGE in December 1997 and the versioned dialects died with it.

The second attempt was Mozilla's, roughly 2006–2012:

<script type="application/javascript;version=1.8">

which gated Firefox-only features such as generator expressions. No other browser implemented it, so using it meant writing Firefox-only pages. Mozilla removed it. Since then the position has been explicit and unanimous: there will never be a version selector for JavaScript.

So the correction to your model is this. It is not that old versions keep working alongside new ones. There is only ever one version, it is whatever the browser shipped this morning, and every page ever written must run correctly under it. A page from 1997 and a page written today are handed to the same parser, the same engine, the same semantics. That is a far stronger constraint than versioning, and it is why the consequences in the catalogue below are as severe as they are.

One exception exists and it is instructive, because it shows how narrow the escape is. "use strict" (ES5, December 2009) is a version selector of a kind — but look at its shape:

"use strict";
// or, inside one function:
function f() { "use strict"; ... }

It is a string literal. In every engine that predates ES5, that line is an expression statement that evaluates a string and discards it — a complete no-op. So the opt-in is invisible to old engines by construction, which is the only reason it could be added at all. That is the entire trick: the version marker had to be something that already existed and already did nothing. And even then, strict mode is a small set of changes — it cannot remove var, cannot fix typeof null, cannot change ==. It removes a handful of the most dangerous behaviours and stops.

The second exception is modules, and it uses the same logic at a larger scale. Module code is strict by default. Why is that allowed? Because import and export were syntax errors before ES2015, so no existing file can possibly be a module. A file loaded as a module is new territory by definition, so the committee could set better defaults inside it for free. Modules are strict, their top-level this is undefined rather than the global object, and their declarations do not leak to the global scope — three fixes that could never have been applied to scripts, applied wholesale to modules because modules had no history to protect.

Section 2 — What the constraint is, and who actually enforces it

Here is the thing that surprises most people: there is no rule. Search ECMA-262 for a clause saying "do not break existing code" and you will not find one. It is not a specification requirement. It is not a policy document. It is a market fact, and it is enforced in a place you would not expect.

The enforcement chain runs like this.

1. Browser vendors will not ship changes that break sites, because a browser that breaks sites loses users to one that does not. This is not hypothetical caution; it is measured. Chrome, Firefox and Safari all instrument their engines with use counters — telemetry that records how many page loads across the entire web touch a given API or syntax form. When a change is proposed, the question is not "is this better?" but "what fraction of page loads would change behaviour?" The informal threshold used at Chrome for removing a feature has historically been on the order of 0.03% of page loads, and even that is contested, because 0.03% of the web is millions of pages including, invariably, someone's payroll system.

2. TC39 — the committee that standardises the language — anticipates that refusal. A proposal that browsers will not ship is a dead proposal, so web compatibility is now a first-class part of the process. Proposals routinely arrive with evidence gathered from the HTTP Archive, which crawls several million real sites monthly and stores their scripts, so a proposer can literally grep the web for the pattern they are about to change. The phrase used in these discussions, constantly and without irony, is "don't break the web."

3. The constraint is one-directional and permanent. Adding is nearly free; changing and removing are nearly impossible. Not because anyone forbids it, but because the cost is borne by the browser that goes first, and the benefit is diffuse.

And the reason it bites harder for JavaScript than for anything else is the point from Resolution 1, Part 5, now sharpened: the web has no update path and no dependency declaration. A published page is a build with no build system. Its author may be dead. Its server may be a machine nobody has logged into in fifteen years. It cannot be recompiled, repackaged or patched. There is no equivalent of "bump the major version and let people upgrade," because there is nobody to do the upgrading.

Section 3 — How you grow a language you are not allowed to change: four hatches

Everything in the catalogue is an instance of one of these four moves. Learning them lets you predict, on sight, why a new feature has the shape it has.

Hatch 1 — Use syntax that was previously an error. If a construct used to be a syntax error, no existing page can depend on it, so its meaning is free real estate. This is the safest hatch and it is where most modern syntax comes from: class, =>, template literals (the backtick was previously invalid anywhere outside a string), destructuring, spread ..., async/await, generators, #private fields.

But even here the old grammar reaches up and constrains the new. The best example is optional chaining, ES2020. You would think ?. was free. It was not, because this was already legal:

x ? .5 : 1        // a conditional whose consequent is the number .5

Tokenised naively, x?.5:1 now begins with the token ?. and the whole expression becomes a syntax error — silently changing the meaning of existing code. So the specification carries an explicit lookahead restriction: ?. is only the optional-chaining token when the next character is not a decimal digit. A punctuation mark in a 2020 feature has a special case in it to protect a numeric literal shorthand from 1995.

The same pressure explains why # was chosen for private fields rather than the obvious private x. Class bodies needed a way to distinguish this.x (public, possibly inherited, possibly a proxy trap) from a truly private slot, decidable at parse time, with no possibility that an existing property name collides. A sigil that was previously illegal is the only thing that gives you that.

Hatch 2 — Pick a name nobody has taken. Adding a method to a built-in prototype is genuinely dangerous, because pages have been adding their own methods to those same prototypes since 1996 and the page's version wins during page setup but loses afterward — or worse, the page's library detects the native one and behaves differently. Section 8 has the incident where this actually happened.

Hatch 3 — Add a parallel thing rather than fixing the broken thing. When a behaviour cannot be changed, the answer is a second API with the right behaviour, and the broken one stays forever beside it. Almost half the catalogue in Section 5 is this move.

Hatch 4 — Add an out-of-band channel. Symbol exists partly for this. If the language wants a hook — "how do I iterate this object?" — putting it at a string key like obj.iterator risks colliding with someone's data. So the hook lives at Symbol.iterator, a value that cannot collide with any string key because it is not a string. Well-known symbols are, in part, a backwards-compatibility device: a namespace that was empty because it did not previously exist.

Section 4 — The catalogue, part one: broken things that were left broken

These are defects that everyone agrees are defects, that have been formally proposed for repair, and that were rejected because repairing them would change the behaviour of existing pages.

typeof null === "object". The cause is an implementation detail of the 1995 engine. Values were stored as a tagged word: a few low bits held a type tag, the rest held the payload. The tag for "object" was 000, and the null value was represented as the machine null pointer — all zero bits. So the tag check on null read 000 and answered "object." It is not a design decision at all; it is a leaked representation. A fix (typeof null === "null") was proposed in the ES4 era and again during ES6 discussions and rejected both times, because a very large amount of code in the wild is written as if (typeof x === "object") with a null check afterward, and flipping the answer changes which branch such code takes. A bug in a ten-day prototype, permanent since.

==. The coercing equality operator's rules — 0 == "0", 0 == [], "0" != [], null == undefined but null != 0 — cannot be changed. Not softened, not tightened. The response was Hatch 3: === was added beside it, and both are in the language forever. Every style guide, every linter rule, every code review comment telling you to use === exists because the original could not be repaired.

Automatic semicolon insertion. The parser, on hitting a token that cannot continue the current statement, inserts a semicolon and tries again. This was deliberate — Section 5 of Resolution 2 explains the audience it was for — and it is unremovable, because millions of pages omit semicolons and depend on the recovery. The permanent consequence is the class of bugs where ASI fires when you did not want it:

function f() {
  return
    { ok: true };
}
f();   // undefined — a semicolon was inserted after `return`

var and function-scoped hoisting. Cannot be removed, cannot be changed. let and const were added beside it in ES2015, which is why you have three declaration forms for one concept — and which is the direct answer to something you will hit again in Node 3.

And let itself is not even a proper keyword, which is a consequence worth seeing. Because let was a perfectly legal identifier before 2015, this is still valid JavaScript today in a non-strict script:

var let = 5;
console.log(let + 1);   // 6

So let is reserved only in strict mode, and in sloppy mode the parser must disambiguate by lookahead: let x = 1 is a declaration, let = 1 is an assignment to a variable named let, and let[0] = 1 is genuinely ambiguous (declaration with array destructuring, or index assignment on an array named let?) and is resolved by a special rule. That is what the constraint costs at the level of grammar.

The global object and var. At the top level of a script, var x = 1 creates a property on the global object, so window.x works. This is a 1995 design that leaks every top-level variable into a shared namespace, and it cannot be changed for scripts. It was changed for modules, per Section 1.

with. A statement that puts an object's properties into scope, making it impossible to know statically what any identifier in the block refers to — hostile to both readers and optimisers. It could not be removed. Strict mode makes it a syntax error, so it survives, live, in every non-strict script on the web.

arguments, arguments.callee, Function.prototype.caller. Same shape: too widely used to remove, dangerous enough to forbid in strict mode. callee and caller are "poisoned" — accessing them in strict mode throws — rather than deleted.

Legacy octal literals. In a sloppy-mode script, 010 is 8, not 10, because a leading zero meant octal in C and JavaScript copied it. Unfixable. Strict mode makes it a syntax error, and ES2015 added the explicit 0o10 form as the sanctioned way to write it. Three spellings of one idea, again.

Array.prototype.sort with no comparator sorts by string.

[1, 10, 2, 20].sort()   // [1, 10, 2, 20]

Every element is converted to a string and compared lexicographically. This is a genuine mistake and it is unfixable, because pages sort arrays without a comparator and rely on the result.

Sparse arrays and array holes. [1, , 3] has a hole at index 1, which is distinct from undefined: 1 in [1, , 3] is false, and forEach skips it while for...of yields undefined. Arrays are objects with numeric string keys, so holes are simply absent keys. This complicates every array method's specification permanently, and each new method (flat, includes, findLast) has to make and document a hole-handling decision.

NaN !== NaN. This one is not JavaScript's fault — it is IEEE 754, and every language with doubles has it. It appears here because of what was done about it: rather than changing ===, Object.is was added in ES2015 as a separate comparison with the sensible answer. Hatch 3 again, applied to a defect JavaScript did not even create.

document.all — the most extraordinary entry in the catalogue. Recall from Resolution 2 that IE4 exposed document.all, and that 1997–2003 pages sniffed for it: if (document.all) { /* IE path */ }. When those pages were later opened in browsers that had implemented the standard DOM, they needed document.all to be falsy — otherwise every one of them would take the ancient IE branch and break. But document.all is an object, and objects are truthy.

The resolution is not a browser hack. It is written into the ECMAScript standard itself. ECMA-262 defines an internal slot named [[IsHTMLDDA]] — "document dot all" — and objects carrying it are specified to be falsy in boolean contexts, to return "undefined" from typeof, and to be loosely equal to both null and undefined:

typeof document.all        // "undefined"
document.all == null       // true
Boolean(document.all)      // false
document.all               // ...but it is a real object that works

The type system of the language has a bespoke exception carved into it for one property of one browser, to protect pages written in 1998. If you want a single artefact that proves how absolute this constraint is, that is it.

Section 5 — The catalogue, part two: things that exist only as workarounds

Everything here is Hatch 3 — a second API added because the first could not be repaired. Read this list as a map of the language's unfixable defects, seen from the other side.

===== could not be fixed
let / const (ES2015)var's function scoping and hoisting could not be fixed
Object.is (ES2015)=== could not be changed for NaN and -0
for...of (ES2015)for...in walks inherited enumerable string keys and could not be changed
Object.keys / values / entriessame defect, approached from the object side
Map and Set (ES2015)plain objects have string-only keys and inherit from Object.prototype; that could not be changed, so real collections were added beside them
Object.create(null)every object literal inherits Object.prototype, so {}["toString"] is a function; using an object as a lookup table needed an escape
Object.hasOwn (ES2022)obj.hasOwnProperty(k) breaks when obj is Object.create(null) or has a property literally named hasOwnProperty; the method could not be made safe, so a static one was added
Array.prototype.includes (ES2016)indexOf uses ===, so it can never find NaN; its semantics could not be changed
String.prototype.replaceAll (ES2021)replace with a string pattern replaces only the first occurrence; a thirty-year-old surprise, fixed by addition
Number.isNaN, Number.isFinite, Number.parseInt (ES2015)the global isNaN coerces its argument, so isNaN("hello") is true; non-coercing versions were added under a new namespace
BigInt (ES2020)all numbers are IEEE-754 doubles, losing integer precision above 2⁵³; Number could not be changed, so a second numeric type was added — with its own literal syntax (10n) and a deliberate refusal to mix, since 1n + 1 throws rather than silently choosing a precision
globalThis (ES2020)the global object is window in pages, self in workers, global in Node; none could be renamed, so a fourth name was standardised that means "whichever of those you are in"
Symbol (ES2015)any new string-keyed hook could collide with page data; a non-string key space was needed
Modules (ES2015)scripts could not be made strict, could not stop leaking to the global object, could not get a sane top-level this; a new file type inherited all three fixes at once
Temporal (shipping from 2025)the whole of Date — this is the largest one

Date deserves its own paragraph, because it is the clearest demonstration of the constraint's cost. Date was copied from java.util.Date in 1995 in Eich's ten days, and it inherited every flaw that Java itself abandoned in 1997. Months are 0-indexed while days are 1-indexed, so new Date(2026, 8, 28) is September. Objects are mutable, so passing a date to a function that calls setDate silently modifies your copy. Parsing anything that is not an ISO 8601 string is implementation-defined, so new Date("03/04/2026") can legitimately differ between browsers. There is no way to represent a date without a time, or a time without a date, or an instant in a named time zone.

None of it can be fixed. Every one of those behaviours is depended on somewhere. So the answer, after thirty years, is Temporal — an entirely new global namespace with Temporal.PlainDate, Temporal.ZonedDateTime, Temporal.Duration and the rest, all immutable, all explicit about time zones. It reached Stage 3 and began shipping in browsers from 2025. And Date does not go away. It stays, working exactly as it did in 1995, forever, beside its replacement.

Section 6 — Annex B: the constraint given a name and a filing cabinet

You asked for each and everything, and there is a place where the language keeps the worst of it, formally, in the standard. Annex B of ECMA-262 is titled "Additional ECMAScript Features for Web Browsers." Its own introduction says the features in it are not part of the core language and are not recommended, and that they are documented only because web browsers cannot remove them without breaking existing content. It is marked normative optional: not required of a general ECMAScript implementation, required in practice of any browser.

It is, in other words, an official list of things the language regrets. Contents include:

HTML-like comments in JavaScript source. Recall the 1996 trick from Resolution 1, where script bodies were wrapped in <!-- and // --> so browsers with no <script> support would not print the code as text. Enough pages did this, and enough of them omitted the leading //, that <!-- and --> had to be specified as legal comment syntax inside JavaScript itself. A workaround for browsers that no longer exist, for a problem that no longer exists, is permanent grammar.

__proto__. A SpiderMonkey extension exposing an object's prototype as a magic property. Never designed, never standardised, used everywhere. ES2015 was forced to specify it — including the fact that { "__proto__": x } in an object literal sets the prototype while { ["__proto__"]: x } creates an ordinary property. Object.getPrototypeOf and Object.setPrototypeOf are the sanctioned replacements, and __proto__ stays.

escape and unescape. Broken URL encoders from 1995 that mishandle non-ASCII. Replaced by encodeURIComponent in ES3, 1999. Still present, twenty-seven years later.

The string HTML methods. "hi".bold() returns "<b>hi</b>". There is also .big(), .small(), .blink(), .fontcolor(), .anchor(), .link(). These generate markup that HTML itself deprecated decades ago. String.prototype.blink is in the ECMAScript standard in 2026.

Date.prototype.getYear and setYear. The Y2K-era methods that return the year minus 1900. getYear() today returns 126.

String.prototype.substr — the one with a length rather than an end index, which is why you can never remember whether you want substr, substring or slice. Deprecated in Annex B; universally supported.

RegExp.prototype.compile, __defineGetter__, __defineSetter__, __lookupGetter__, __lookupSetter__ — all superseded by Object.defineProperty in ES5, all still specified.

And a set of semantic patches, not just leftover functions. Annex B also specifies web-compatible behaviour for things that are genuinely ambiguous in the core grammar — most notably what a function declaration inside a block means in sloppy mode:

if (x) { function f() {} }   // legal, with specified-but-strange scoping,
                             // only because pages did it

and the "legacy octal escape sequences" in string literals, and labelled function declarations. These are not deprecated APIs; they are corrections to the shape of the language made to match what browsers already did.

Section 7 — Your second ask: what could not be done

Now the foreclosed design space, stated directly. Every item is something a designer starting fresh would do, and the language cannot.

It cannot reserve new keywords. This is the largest structural cost and the least visible. Any word you reserve might be an identifier in an existing page. So since ES3 in 1999, JavaScript has added almost no genuinely reserved words. Instead it has contextual keywords — words that are keywords in one position and identifiers everywhere else. All of these are legal today:

var async = 1;          // `async` is not reserved
var of = 2;             // `of` in for...of is not reserved
var get = 3, set = 4;   // contextual, in object literals and classes
var from = 5;           // `from` in import statements is not reserved
var target = 6;         // as in new.target
var let = 7;            // legal in sloppy mode (Section 4)
var yield = 8;          // legal outside generators, in sloppy mode
var await = 9;          // legal in a sloppy script, illegal in a module

That last one is worth staring at. await is a reserved word only in modules and inside async functions — the same eight characters are an identifier in one file and a keyword in another, determined by how the file was loaded. The parser must therefore track a "goal symbol" and a set of grammar parameters, and the specification's grammar is festooned with annotations like [+Await] and [~Yield] that switch productions on and off. The published grammar of JavaScript is substantially more complicated than the language it describes, and the complexity is almost entirely this.

It cannot change any operator's semantics. Not ==, not +'s overload between addition and concatenation, not the coercion rules, not typeof's answers. Operators are the highest-traffic surface in the language and therefore the most frozen.

It cannot make the language strict by default. Only opt in, per file or per function, or per new file type.

It cannot remove a built-in. Not one, in thirty-one years — see Section 8.

It cannot freely add methods to built-in prototypes, because libraries have been squatting on those namespaces since 1996. The committee's own vocabulary is limited by what other people's code has already claimed. Section 8 is where this stopped being theoretical.

It cannot introduce a real integer type, or fix numeric precision, or change division to be exact. BigInt is a parallel type precisely because Number is immovable — and the deliberate refusal to let BigInt and Number mix in arithmetic exists so that the split is loud rather than silently lossy.

It cannot make objects non-inheriting, arrays non-sparse, or properties non-configurable by default. Each default is depended on.

It cannot fix Date. Only stand a second date library beside it.

And it cannot even control its own extension points cleanly. The DOM, the browser APIs, and the language share one global object, so every new global name — fetch, Promise, Proxy, globalThis, structuredClone — is a name that might already be taken by a page. Each addition is a compatibility decision, and several have been renamed or delayed for exactly that reason.

Section 8 — The times it actually broke, and what they prove

Three episodes, because they show the constraint being tested rather than asserted.

SmooshGate, 2018 — the definitive case. TC39 was standardising a method to flatten nested arrays, named the obvious thing: Array.prototype.flatten. Firefox shipped it in a nightly build. Sites broke immediately.

The cause was MooTools, a JavaScript library that was extremely popular around 2007–2011 and is still present on a long tail of unmaintained sites. MooTools added its own Array.prototype.flatten, and it did so with a guard of roughly this shape:

// paraphrase of the MooTools pattern
if (!Array.prototype.flatten) {
  Array.prototype.flatten = function () { ... };
}

Once browsers provided a native flatten, the guard saw one already there and skipped its own definition — but the native version had different semantics from MooTools', and every site using MooTools' behaviour broke. Note the trap: the library was written defensively, and the defence is what failed.

The committee's response was not to argue that the sites should be fixed. It was to rename the method. Array.prototype.flatten became Array.prototype.flat, which is why the method you use has a slightly odd name. (The nickname comes from an alternative proposal, half-serious, to call it smoosh.)

The same library had caused the same problem five years earlier: String.prototype.contains collided with MooTools and was renamed String.prototype.includes. Two of the method names you type regularly are the shape they are because of one library from 2008.

parseInt and octal, ES5, 2009 — a change that was allowed. Under ES3, an implementation was permitted (not required) to treat a leading zero as octal, so parseInt("08") returned 0 in some browsers and 8 in others. ES5 removed the permission and mandated base 10. This was allowed to change precisely because it had never been consistent: no correct code could have depended on it, since there was no single behaviour to depend on.

Stable sort, ES2019 — the same principle. Array.prototype.sort's stability was previously unspecified, and engines differed (V8 used insertion sort for short arrays and an unstable quicksort for long ones). ES2019 mandated stability. Again: what was unspecified could be pinned down, because nothing was entitled to rely on it.

The rule these three reveal is more precise than "nothing can change." It is:

Specified behaviour is frozen. Unspecified or inconsistent behaviour can be fixed — and fixing it usually means standardising on whatever the majority of engines already did.

That is the only real crack in the wall, and it is how a surprising amount of cleanup has actually happened.

What has not happened is worth saying plainly, as the answer to your question about what the constraint has cost: in thirty-one years, ECMAScript has never removed a feature that pages depend on. Not one. Annex B exists for exactly this reason — so that the committee can say "this is bad, do not use it" without ever saying "this is gone."

Section 9 — What it costs, and what it buys

The cost is everything above, and one thing more: an entire industry of tooling exists to paper over it. TypeScript exists largely to restore the type discipline that == and implicit coercion cannot have. ESLint's default recommended ruleset is substantially a list of "do not use the parts we could not remove." Babel exists because new syntax must be translated back into the old language for engines that predate it. Bundlers exist partly because modules arrived seventeen years late. None of those tools would be necessary in a language that had been allowed to fix itself.

And the benefit is exactly one thing, but it is enormous:

A page written in 1996 still works in a browser released this year.

Hold that against the alternatives.
